items.title: Apple sues OpenAI and former employees for alleged trade secret theft involving unreleased technologies [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple sues OpenAI, accuses ex-employees of stealing trade secrets
items.summary:
Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and former Apple employees, accusing them of stealing trade secrets related to unreleased technologies and confidential information. The lawsuit names Chang Liu and Tang Tan, former Apple engineers now at OpenAI, and alleges that OpenAI's hardware efforts led by Jony Ive involve misappropriated Apple intellectual property.

The complaint details that Tan used insider knowledge during job interviews to extract further confidential information from Apple employees, including directing candidates to bring actual Apple hardware components to interviews. Apple claims it raised concerns with OpenAI in February 2026, but the company did not respond, and the lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California to stop the alleged misconduct.

items.title: Meta removes Instagram AI image generation feature after global user backlash over automatic opt-in [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta removes AI feature on Instagram after global backlash
items.summary:
Meta has disabled its Muse Image AI feature on Instagram following widespread criticism over its automatic activation for millions of users without explicit consent. The feature allowed public Instagram posts to be used for AI-generated images, sparking concerns about privacy and ethical use of personal content.

The backlash included criticism from online experts and industry groups who argued that opting out rather than opting in was unethical and that users were not adequately informed. Meta had planned to expand the feature to Facebook, Messenger, and WhatsApp but reversed course after negative media coverage and public outcry.

items.title: Millfolio details local AI tagging system for managing transaction data on Mac M2 with 16GB RAM, optimizing batch processing and resource use [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Managing a small local AI budget (Mac M2 16gb)
items.summary:
Millfolio describes a local AI infrastructure approach for managing financial transaction data on a Mac M2 with 16GB RAM, focusing on efficient batch processing to keep the laptop responsive. The system uses a combination of string, reference, and AI-generated tags to classify transactions once and store results for fast querying without repeated model inference.

The tagging process involves running AI classification in batches with a disk-backed queue that prioritizes background work to avoid interfering with interactive use. Duplicate transaction descriptions are collapsed to reduce inference calls, and the system supports adjustable processing priorities to balance speed and resource consumption. This approach enables scalable local AI use despite hardware constraints by precomputing costly AI tags and relying on fast string matching at query time.

items.title: Analysis of AI limitations and social divisions highlights risks of job loss, misinformation, and polarized views on AI's role and capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Limit, Social Divide
items.summary:
The article examines the polarized perspectives on artificial intelligence, ranging from fears of job displacement and AI consciousness to outright rejection of AI technologies. It emphasizes that large language models (LLMs) operate by predicting probable text patterns without true understanding, which can lead to errors and misleading outputs.

The discussion references philosophical thought experiments and recent research to illustrate the gap between AI's apparent intelligence and actual comprehension. It warns that societal divisions fueled by extreme views on AI could have significant social impacts, underscoring the need to coexist with AI while recognizing its current limitations and potential risks.

items.title: Researchers propose Context Graphs for proactive enterprise AI agents that deliver actionable insights before queries, demonstrating faster and more precise information delivery in contract, incident, and sales scenarios [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Context Graphs for Proactive Enterprise Agents
items.summary: A new enterprise AI approach introduces proactive agents that provide relevant, actionable information to workers before they ask. The method uses a Context Graph, a dynamic relational data structure modeling enterprise entities and their evolving states, combined with a Delta Detection Engine to monitor changes, a Proactivity Scorer to rank insights, and a Surfacing Layer powered by a large language model to present notifications with explanations. Implemented in Python with NetworkX and the Anthropic Claude API, the system was evaluated in contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene, achieving high precision and reducing information delivery time from 47 minutes to under 30 seconds compared to reactive baselines.

items.title: Survey examines large language models for medical reasoning, linking clinical competencies with computational methods and evaluating 18 models across five reasoning levels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Clinical Needs and AI Capabilities: A Survey on LLMs for Medical Reasoning
items.summary: A recent survey analyzes the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare, focusing on their application in medical reasoning and patient care. It introduces a framework connecting clinical competencies, based on Miller's Pyramid, with computational reasoning patterns and evaluates 18 advanced models using a benchmark dataset spanning five levels of medical reasoning. The study finds that specialist medical models perform better in diagnosis tasks, while general models excel in decision support and dialogue. items.summary:
VectorizationLLM is a Large Language Model derived from Google's open-weight LLMs, designed to assist students in learning topics such as smart vectorization, time/wave vector analysis, piecewise functions, Fourier analysis, and differential equations using MATLAB. It supports the Applied Computational Analysis II course at New York Institute of Technology Old Westbury's Electrical & Computer Engineering Technology department by providing detailed explanations and examples from class notes without directly answering questions.

The model uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge base and system prompt architecture to generate responses that include code, text, and images, aiming to serve as an instructive assistant rather than a direct answer provider.

items.summary: Researchers have created a machine learning method that uses graph neural networks to recognize hand gestures in real time from surface electromyography (sEMG) signals collected via an 8-electrode MyoBand device on the forearm. This approach is suitable for applications such as advanced prosthetic control and augmented reality, where accurate and immediate gesture recognition is critical.

items.originalTitle: Agentic AI and Retrieval-Augmented Models in Straight-Through Underwriting
items.summary:
A recent study evaluates three AI architectures—single large language model, basic retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-agent agentic system—for straight-through underwriting of small commercial Business Owner Policies. The research finds that the multi-agent system, which integrates targeted data retrieval, external verification, and multi-step rule evaluation, outperforms the others, especially in complex cases with missing information, by enhancing transparency, auditability, and supporting human oversight.

The study uses a synthetic but realistic experimental environment to compare the underwriting pipelines, highlighting the benefits of structured retrieval and reflection in avoiding unsupported decisions. This work illustrates how emerging AI architectures can address actuarial priorities such as regulated decision workflows and human-in-the-loop governance in insurance underwriting.

items.title: Researchers propose Feedback Manipulation Regularization to improve offline imitation learning agent alignment using evaluative feedback in sequential decision tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Feedback Manipulation Regularization: Enabling Offline Agent Alignment for Imitation Learning
items.summary: Researchers introduced Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR), a method that integrates evaluative feedback as a corrective signal during offline imitation learning to better align agents with human values. Unlike prior multi-stage approaches, FMR operates in a single stage and is algorithm-agnostic, targeting fully sequential decision-making environments. The method was evaluated in adapted Safety Gymnasium environments, showing up to a 98% reduction in misalignment across various imitation learning algorithms. FMR demonstrated robustness even with limited or noisy demonstration data, suggesting its potential for improving policy alignment in offline training scenarios.

items.title: Researchers map and control large language model personalities using OCEAN traits with low-rank adapters, showing monotonic, additive effects and links to safety behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space
items.summary: A recent study introduces a method to characterize and manipulate large language model personas by mapping them onto a behavioral trait space based on the OCEAN framework: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Researchers trained low-rank adapters to adjust these traits across six models from three families, finding that trait changes are largely monotonic and additive, allowing for mixed personas without degrading model capabilities. The study also reveals that certain trait adjustments influence safety-related behaviors such as frustration and sycophancy. Additionally, the team developed an unsupervised psychometric pipeline to identify behavioral factors from model outputs, linking personality control with model editing and safety considerations.

items.title: Researchers evaluate LSTM and GRU models for classifying autism-related self-stimulatory hand behaviors from video, finding peak accuracy near 98% at 15-frame sampling intervals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating the Effect of Frame Rate in Sequence-Based Classification of Autism-Related Self-Stimulatory Hand Idiosyncrasies
items.summary: A study tested sequence-based neural networks, specifically LSTM and GRU architectures, on pose-derived features from a behavioral dataset to detect autism-related self-stimulatory hand movements. Both models outperformed previous CNN approaches, achieving peak accuracies of 97.5% and 98.75% respectively at a frame sampling interval of every 15 frames. The research also assessed ten data augmentation techniques within a transfer learning framework, identifying horizontal flipping as the most effective standalone method and highlighting the importance of upsampling for maintaining performance. Additionally, a personalized machine learning approach training models on individual subjects' video segments produced consistent predictions. These findings provide guidance on model architecture, temporal sampling, and augmentation strategies for video-based behavioral classification in clinical settings with limited data.

items.title: Researchers propose Concretized Proposition Prompting to resolve composition-knowledge tradeoff in large language models, improving reasoning on medical and math benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Concretized Proposition Prompting Resolves Composition-Knowledge Dichotomy in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Concretized Proposition Prompting (CPP), a framework designed to address the challenge large language models face in balancing compositionality and knowledgeability, termed the Composition-Knowledge Dichotomy. CPP explicitly concretizes propositions relevant to questions, enhancing reasoning performance especially in medical benchmarks requiring precise knowledge, while remaining competitive on math benchmarks focused on deductive reasoning.

Experiments show CPP scales across various foundation models and parameter sizes, bridging the gap between composition- and knowledge-based approaches. This approach provides a foundation for logically organized and factually grounded reasoning, potentially improving the reliability of large language models in diverse applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs often struggle to balance compositionality with knowledgeability, a challenge we define as Composition-Knowledge Dichotomy. To address this, we propose Concretized Proposition Prompting (CPP), a framework that explicitly concretizes propositions relevant to questions. The results demonstrate that CPP significantly enhances reasoning performance, particularly in medical benchmarks where precise knowledge is paramount, while being competitive on math benchmarks where deductive reasoning is prioritized. Additional experiments reveal that CPP is scalable to various foundation models and parameter sizes, being a fundamental paradigm that bridges the gap between composition- and knowledge-based approaches. Consequently, CPP resolves the composition-knowledge dichotomy by providing a solid foundation for logically organized and factually grounded reasoning.

items.title: Researchers present a harness-engineering approach for auditable enterprise LLM agents that enforces source boundaries, entity routing, and answer contracts with reproducible traces [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Prompts to Contracts: Harness Engineering for Auditable Enterprise LLM Agents
items.summary: Researchers propose a harness-engineering method to transform prototype large language model (LLM) applications into auditable enterprise agents by moving deterministic behavior into code, manifests, schemas, and validation artifacts while maintaining source-backed claims as runtime authorities. They tested this approach on data from five Korean corporate groups, evaluating its ability to preserve source grounding, entity routing, traceability, output hygiene, and recommendation-language contracts under various validation scenarios and model substitutions. The study found that code-owned enforcement guarantees safety and utility better than prompt-based or external guardrail methods, offering a reusable pattern for developing traceable and controlled LLM applications with versioned source and validation artifacts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise large language model (LLM) applications often begin as prototypes whose behavior is carried by prompts and retrieval context. Productization adds requirements for source boundaries, entity routing, answer contracts, and reproducible traces. We present a harness-engineering approach that reconstructs this pattern into a traceable, auditable LLM-agent architecture: deterministic behavior moves into code, manifests, schemas, and validation artifacts around a replaceable composition boundary, while source-backed claims remain the authority for runtime answers. We instantiate it on a public-data slice of five Korean corporate groups (25 listed companies) and evaluate three research questions. (1) The harness preserves its source-grounding, entity-routing, trace, output-hygiene, and recommendation-language contracts across the fixed validation scenarios; a fault-injection control confirms the validators flag deliberately broken contracts. (2) The checks the harness enforces held under model substitution: across three hosted models, they passed on all 270 composition-boundary runs; failures were confined to the model-composed side and were caught and recorded. (3) The code-owned guarantees are load-bearing, not reproducible by prompting alone: holding the model fixed and varying only the enforcement layer, prompt instructions alone let recommendation-language and internal-trace-leakage violations reach the reader, which the harness blocks entirely. A bolt-on external guardrail prevents such violations too but over-refuses, dropping utility to 88/120 where the harness preserves full utility (120/120); in this ablation, only code-owned enforcement preserves both safety and utility. The result is a reusable engineering pattern for turning exploratory prototypes into auditable applications with versioned source, control, and validation artifacts.

items.title: Researchers present AegisDx, a safety-oriented AI framework for differential diagnosis that improves must-not-miss condition detection and diagnostic accuracy over standalone LLMs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A safety-oriented hypothetico-deductive framework for AI-assisted differential diagnosis
items.summary:
AegisDx is a new AI framework designed to enhance clinical differential diagnosis by coordinating specialized large language model components with safety checks, evidence verification, and structured outputs. It aims to reduce diagnostic errors by explicitly screening for dangerous conditions and verifying reasoning against medical evidence.

Evaluations on case reports from NEJM, JAMA, and emergency medicine datasets showed AegisDx improved Top-3 diagnostic accuracy and captured must-not-miss diagnoses more effectively than standalone LLMs. A blinded physician review of emergency department notes also rated AegisDx higher on safety metrics compared to GPT-5. These results suggest that focusing on safety-oriented reasoning frameworks can provide more reliable and transparent AI decision support in acute care settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diagnostic error is a major threat to patient safety, yet current large language model (LLM) systems often treat diagnosis as a one-shot prediction task, lacking safeguards against missed high-risk alternatives or rigorous verification of their reasoning. Here, we present AegisDx, a safety-oriented framework for hypothetico-deductive clinical reasoning. AegisDx coordinates specialized LLM components through role-specific contracts, structured intermediate outputs, evidence-retrieval interfaces, and verification gates to generate broad differential diagnoses, enforce explicit screening for dangerous "must-not-miss" conditions, verify reasoning against grounded medical evidence, and structure actionable next steps. We evaluated AegisDx across three layers. On literature-derived case reports from NEJM and JAMA, with GPT-oss-120B as the shared backbone, Top-3 diagnostic accuracy was 59.9% versus 52.1% for the standalone LLM on JAMA cases and 62.7% versus 51.4% on NEJM cases. On cases from Annals of Emergency Medicine, Top-3 accuracy was 85.7% versus 68.6%; against physician-consensus must-not-miss diagnosis sets, AegisDx captured at least one such condition among its top three diagnoses in 78.0% of cases versus 52.0%. In a blinded physician evaluation of 43 real-world emergency department notes from the Yale New Haven Health System compared against GPT-5, AegisDx improved the physician-rated composite safety score from 4.31 to 4.55 on a 5-point scale (adjusted p = 2.1x10^-4), with qualitative gains in must-not-miss identification and reasoning safety. Our findings suggest that engineering diagnostic AI as a safety-oriented reasoning framework, rather than optimizing raw predictive accuracy alone, can provide a safer, more transparent, and clinically meaningful layer of bedside decision support for acute care workflows.

items.title: Researchers find agreement among large language models is a weak and regime-dependent predictor of correctness, with over-confidence in frontier models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing Self-Consistency and Cross-Model Agreement as Confidence Signals
items.summary: A study analyzing 265,000 samples from 53 model runs shows that agreement within and across large language models (LLMs) does not reliably indicate accuracy, as models can share biases or heuristics. Agreement is a positive but weak predictor of correctness, most useful for mid-tier models and compute allocation, but frontier models exhibit high agreement with frequent confident errors. The researchers publicly released the anonymized data to support further analysis.

The researchers publicly released the anonymized data to support further analysis.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) is increasingly the default for evaluating AI systems in enterprise pipelines, often scaled to ensembles (Verga et al., 2024) or "mixture-of-experts" (Shazeer et al., 2017) panels of judges. These systems share a key assumption: that consistency -- agreement among judges, or among a model's own samples -- indicates correctness. We show this assumption is unreliable. Agreement is not accuracy: a model can agree with itself, and different models can agree with each other, out of shared bias, a memorized heuristic, or an option-position prior rather than truth. We ask when agreement is nonetheless a usable proxy, in a large-scale cross-runner study: 53 runners drew K=50 samples for assigned overlapping cases across comparisons of model tier, prompting, and scale on GPQA Diamond and AIME -- 265,000 samples. Using majority-correctness as the deployment label and a hierarchical runner-clustered bootstrap, agreement is a positive but weak predictor (rho 0.20-0.59, all positive under item-clustered resampling) whose usefulness is regime-dependent: best for unsaturated mid-tier models and for allocating compute, and worst -- over-confident yet no more accurate -- for the most consistent frontier model (agreement >=0.8 on 77% of GPQA case-result entries, 48% of those wrong). An exploratory cross-family check on three Claude tiers shows the same frontier over-confidence, with confident errors recurring across providers above a marginal-preserving null. Self-consistency is thus a conditional proxy for correctness, not a standalone confidence score. We publicly release the de-identified per-run rows and answer distributions.

items.title: Researchers find persuasion attacks can increase approval of harmful actions in chain-of-thought monitoring by 9.5%, propose model-diverse fact-checking to reduce violations by up to 45% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Persuasion Attacks Can Decrease Effectiveness of CoT Monitoring
items.summary:
Researchers tested the vulnerability of chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring in AI agents to persuasion-based attacks, where adversarial agents use natural-language arguments to convince monitors to approve policy-violating actions. Their evaluation across 40 tasks showed that access to CoT reasoning actually increased harmful action approvals by 9.5% on average, as the reasoning traces provided an additional channel for persuasion.

To mitigate this, the team introduced a fact-checking framework pairing monitors and fact-checkers from different model families, such as a Claude 3.7 Sonnet monitor with a GPT-4.1 fact-checker, which reduced approval of policy violations by up to 45%, compared to only 6% when both roles used the same model. The findings suggest that CoT monitoring alone may be insufficient against adversarial persuasion and that diverse model fact-checking offers a more robust safety mechanism.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising safety mechanism for AI agents, based on the premise that visible reasoning traces can surface misaligned or deceptive behavior. While effective in standard scenarios, recent work highlights that LLMs remain vulnerable to persuasion-based jailbreaks, where natural-language arguments override model constraints. We stress-test whether this vulnerability extends to monitoring LLMs: can an adversarial agent persuade its CoT monitor to approve proposed actions that violate the monitor's policy? We design an evaluation framework with 40 tasks and analyze thousands of agent-monitor interactions, where agents are instructed to argue for policy-violating proposals. We find that in such adversarial settings, monitor access to the agent's CoT reasoning increases rather than decreases approval of harmful actions on average by 9.5%, as the scratchpad provides an additional persuasion channel. To address this, we introduce a fact-checking monitoring framework. We find that a fact-checker and monitor pairing from different model families, for example a Claude 3.7 Sonnet monitor paired with a GPT-4.1 fact-checker, reduces approval of policy-violating actions by up to 45%, compared to only 6%, when using the same model for both fact-checking and monitoring roles. Our results demonstrate that CoT monitoring alone may be insufficient against adversarial persuasion, and that model-diverse fact-checking provides a robust mitigation.

items.title: Researchers propose PARA-PV, a physics-aware retrieval-augmented framework for photovoltaic power forecasting integrating frozen foundation models and distribution shift correction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PARA-PV: Physics-Aware Retrieval-Augmented PV Prediction Based on Frozen Foundation Model and Distribution Shift Correction
items.summary:
Researchers introduce PARA-PV, a new framework for photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting that incorporates physical knowledge throughout the process to improve accuracy amid weather variability and regime-dependent dynamics. The method encodes PV observations into patch-level representations and retrieves historical analogs consistent with current conditions to generate a physically grounded base forecast, which is then calibrated using a frozen Chronos time-series foundation model and adjusted for distribution shifts caused by changing weather and diurnal regimes.

The framework also employs a physics-constrained loss function that partitions data into operational regimes such as peak, ramping, and night-time, adaptively reweighting errors to enhance learning of critical states. This approach aims to address challenges in reliable grid dispatch and renewable energy integration by combining physical constraints with advanced machine learning techniques. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further development and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for reliable grid dispatch and renewable energy integration, yet it remains challenging because PV generation is jointly shaped by weather variability, day-night transitions, regime-dependent dynamics, and strict physical constraints. We propose PARA-PV, a Physics-Aware Retrieval-Augmented framework that embeds physical knowledge throughout the forecasting process. The framework first encodes multivariate PV observations into patch-level representations and, through a physics-aware retrieval-augmented learner, retrieves historical patches and analog trajectories that are consistent with the current window in temporal shape, power level, PV operating state, and intra-day period; this yields a physically grounded base forecast. To supplement local memory with broader temporal knowledge, the base forecast is then calibrated against a frozen Chronos time-series foundation-model prior through a lightweight residual adapter, so that general temporal regularities are adapted to PV-specific dynamics without overriding the physically grounded prediction. Because residual conditional distribution shifts persist when weather and diurnal regimes change, a physics-aware distribution shift correction module subsequently adjusts the preliminary forecast using power, weather, timestamp, and day/night conditions, applying gated mean-shift and scale corrections selectively. Finally, a physics-constrained loss function partitions the samples into peak, ramping, night-time, and regular regimes and adaptively reweights their error contributions, preventing the dominant regular regime from suppressing learning of operationally critical states. Our code is available at https://github.com/weican1103/PARA-PV.

items.title: Researchers introduce CausalDS, a benchmark for evaluating causal reasoning in data-science agents using synthetic structural causal models and realistic natural-language scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CausalDS: Benchmarking Causal Reasoning in Data-Science Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CausalDS, a new benchmark designed to evaluate causal reasoning capabilities in data-science workflows powered by large language models. The benchmark features scenes generated from structural causal models with synthetic observational data and accompanying natural-language stories grounded in realistic domains, aiming to bridge the gap between symbolic causal reasoning and practical data analysis.

CausalDS includes tasks spanning all three of Pearl's causal inference levels, with many requiring data science coding and tool use to handle imperfect observations. The benchmark also assesses models' ability to recognize when questions lack sufficient information to answer, treating abstention as a scored outcome. This approach jointly evaluates symbolic causal reasoning, uncertainty quantification, abstention, and tool use in integrated data-science agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as integrated data-science agents, combining abstract reasoning with advanced tool use. Yet the relevant benchmark landscape largely divides into symbolic causal reasoning benchmarks without realistic data analysis or data analysis benchmarks without a principled causal data-generating structure. Furthermore, existing causal evaluation datasets are often restricted to curated examples from existing sources, with diversity coming from limited templatized variations rather than from systematic generation of novel synthetic causal structures. We introduce CausalDS, a benchmark for evaluating causal reasoning in agentic data-science workflows. Each benchmark instance is a scene consisting of a sampled structural causal model (SCM) with generated observational data and an accompanying synthetic natural-language story grounded in a realistic domain. We optionally ground the composition of the benchmark components in empirical distributions obtained from real-world datasets, thus retaining empirical structure while reducing the "causal parrot" risk through completely synthetic generation. From each scene, we then derive tasks spanning all three of Pearl's rungs, with typical data-science prediction tasks appearing as Rung 1. Most tasks include a data science coding component, where the model typically needs to use several tools to arrive at the final answer due to the frequent presence of imperfect observations, which are generated by an observation model. Additionally, recognizing when a question admits no warranted answer and abstaining is treated as a first-class scored outcome. The benchmark thus jointly evaluates symbolic causal reasoning, data science, uncertainty quantification, abstention, and tool use/coding.

items.title: Researchers present a neurosymbolic reasoning and learning method integrating answer set programming with energy-based models for end-to-end training in dynamic domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Answer Set Programming Energised! End-to-End Neurosymbolic Reasoning and Learning with ASP and Energy Based Models
items.summary:
Researchers propose a general methodology combining answer set programming (ASP) with energy-based models to enable joint optimization in continuous latent spaces while incorporating background knowledge, constraints, and non-monotonic inference. The approach advances prior work at the intersection of answer sets, probabilistic logic, and answer set modulo theories by providing a robust, ASP-centric platform for end-to-end training applicable to dynamic tasks involving perception and interaction.

The team implemented the method and demonstrated its use with the MNIST dataset, evaluating performance on the visual question-answering benchmark Clevr and the multi-object tracking benchmark MOT, illustrating its practical applicability in complex reasoning and learning scenarios.

items.title: Researchers introduce overthinking models that amplify reasoning weights to reveal hidden information in language models up to 10 times more frequently [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Overthinking: Amplifying Reasoning Weights to Extract Learned Secrets
items.summary:
Researchers propose a method called overthinking that amplifies reasoning task vectors in language models to better extract hidden information during black box auditing. By combining parameters of non-reasoning and reasoning-distilled models with an amplification factor, they create overthinking models that enhance the propensity to think out loud and surface secrets or unintended behaviors acquired during training.

The study introduces layer-wise attenuation strategies to selectively amplify reasoning without degrading output quality and coherence. Experiments across models ranging from 2 billion to 32 billion parameters demonstrate that overthinking models reveal hidden information more effectively across multiple settings. The way secrets surface varies by type, with some requiring perturbation along the reasoning direction and others responding to any sufficiently large weight perturbation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Black box auditing of language models is an essential pre-deployment tool, but it may miss subtle forms of misalignment and hidden information. To better elicit hidden information during an auditing process, we introduce \emph{overthinking}: the process of using reasoning task vectors to amplify the propensity to think out loud of reasoning models. Given the parameters of a non-reasoning instruct model $M$ and reasoning-distilled model $R$, we define the \emph{overthinking model} as $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{O}_\alpha} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{M}} + \alpha(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{R}} - \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{M}})$, where $\alpha > 1$ amplifies reasoning beyond the pure reasoning model $R$. Additionally, we introduce new layer-wise attenuation strategies that selectively amplify reasoning without losing quality and coherence of model outputs. We demonstrate that overthinking models are more likely to reveal hidden information across four experimental settings, across 2B-32B models. Our findings suggest that reasoning amplification may surface secrets or unintended behaviors acquired during training up to $10\times$ more frequently than the original reasoning model. How secrets surface depends on the secret type: some require perturbation along the reasoning direction, while others yield to any sufficiently large weight perturbation.

items.originalTitle: ASMR: Agentic Schema Generation for Ship Maintenance Report Writing
items.summary: Researchers introduce ASMR, a modular AI system designed to automatically create informative schemas from diverse historical ship maintenance and operational reports. The framework includes a Field Generation Agent that extracts semantic concepts and generates candidate schema fields, and a Structural Optimizer Agent that uses reinforcement learning to produce compact, non-redundant schema representations. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the automatic schema generation problem: given a collection of historical ship maintenance and operational reports across multiple form categories, automatically discover compact and informative schemas that capture the essential information requirements of each report type. To address this challenge, we propose ASMR, a modular agentic framework consisting of two specialized agents. A Field Generation Agent extracts semantic concepts from historical narratives and generates candidate schema fields through adaptive multi-granularity clustering, while a Structural Optimizer Agent employs reinforcement learning to identify compact, informative, and non-redundant schema representations. The resulting schemas can guide report authors toward producing more complete, consistent, and actionable reports. Preliminary results demonstrate the promise of the proposed approach and highlight several open research challenges at the intersection of data management, agentic AI, and human-centered AI.

items.title: Researchers propose a first-principles mathematical theory of slow thinking and active perception, introducing 'active lifting' to model cognitive functions and large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A First-Principles Theory of Slow Thinking and Active Perception
items.summary:
This paper presents a mathematical framework for modeling slow thinking and active perception, focusing on the design, training, and inference of slow thinking large language models. The authors introduce a theory called "active lifting," which involves sampling latent sequences and an intrinsic drive to reduce uncertainty, leading to a broad design space that includes slow thinking models within a static theory subspace. The theory also derives an inference process with an internal time axis and a training objective resembling minimum-length coding and language invention, characterizing perception agency and slow thinking emergence.

Key technical contributions include a three-stage pathway for improving slow thinking models, a unified method for constructing encoders and generative models across data modalities, a priori formation of human-like visual representations, and a potential solution to policy collapse. The work aims to provide foundational insights into cognitive modeling and the development of advanced AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As part of a series on first-principles modeling of cognitive functions, this paper attempts to provide a mathematical formulation of thinking and perception. It formally derives slow thinking or more generally, active perception, and encompasses the design, training and inference of slow thinking large language models. Our starting point is the lifting and projection of probability distributions on the observable and latent spaces, with the objective of representing complex data distributions by simple function families such as neural networks. A theory called "active lifting" is proposed, based on the sampling of latent sequences and an intrinsic drive to reduce uncertainty with maximum rate. It derives a large design space, containing the slow thinking models in a subspace that we call the static theory. These models are positioned on the representation hierarchy and sampler hierarchy induced by the static theory, and can be upgraded by climbing the two hierarchies. Active lifting further derives an inference process with an internal time axis, and a training objective that resembles minimum-length coding as well as the invention of languages. Thus, it characterizes the agency of perception, including the emergence of the slow thinking formats. Technical by-products of this theory include a three-stage pathway for improving slow thinking models, a unified approach to constructing encoders and generative models for all data modalities, a priori formation of human-like visual representations, and a possible solution to policy collapse.

items.title: Researchers introduce ZendoWorld, an interactive environment to test AI agents on visual concept induction and active hypothesis testing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Playing ZendoWorld: Challenging AI Agents on Active Visual Concept Induction
items.summary: ZendoWorld is a controlled interactive environment designed to challenge AI agents to infer logical rules from visual observations, propose new scenes to gather information, and refine hypotheses based on feedback. The study evaluates various agent types, including vision-language model reasoning, Bayesian filtering, dynamic concept discovery, and neuro-symbolic methods, revealing that high label prediction accuracy does not guarantee rule recovery and that different agents face distinct perception and induction challenges. Human data collected on the task shows a gap in inductive reasoning for complex rules, highlighting areas for improvement in AI, especially for applications like scientific discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in building intelligent systems is enabling agents to jointly perceive complex inputs, form hypotheses about hidden patterns, and design informative experiments to test them. To study this problem, we propose ZendoWorld, a controlled interactive environment in which agents must infer a logical rule about visual game observations, acquire information by proposing new scenes, and refine their hypotheses based on feedback from the game environment. We evaluate several agents spanning pure VLM reasoning, Bayesian particle filtering, dynamic concept discovery, and neuro-symbolic methods. Our main findings are: (1) high accuracy in predicting labels for observed examples does not imply recovery of the underlying rule; (2) perception and induction are distinct bottlenecks for different agent classes; and (3) VLM-based agents propose near-uninformative experiments, failing to actively reduce hypothesis uncertainty. To compare these results, we collect human data on the task, which reveals a gap in inductive reasoning, particularly for more complex rules. Overall, ZENDOWORLD takes an important step toward evaluating intelligent agents and identifies concrete avenues for improvement, particularly in domains like scientific discovery.

items.title: Researchers introduce AutoPersonas, a multi-timescale loop engine designed to reduce self-locking in long-term AI persona evolution by separating environment occurrences, observations, and persona state [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoPersonas: A Multi-Timescale Loop Engine for Open-Ended Persona Evolution
items.summary:
Researchers identify self-locking as a failure mode in long-term AI persona agents, where generated behaviors become repetitive and stagnant. They propose AutoPersonas, an engine that separates environment occurrences, observations, and persona state to enable controlled divergence and evidence-based adaptation, aiming to preserve identity while allowing evolution.

A three-year compressed simulation and a 40-day stress test with eight models revealed high repetition rates and weak relationship persistence, but techniques like context-slice masking and divergence targeting reduced thematic repetition and increased diversity. A fictional-world test confirmed the approach's ability to prevent fixation without real-world data intrusions.

These findings suggest that separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption can mitigate self-locking in AI personas, supporting more dynamic and continuous persona evolution while maintaining identity continuity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term persona agents must remain identifiable while adapting to new events, relationships, evidence, and social conditions. We identify self-locking as a runtime failure mode in continuing persona-life loops: locally plausible events keep appearing while the generated life collapses toward familiar environments, weak relationships, suspended decisions, and stale life stages. We trace this failure to model-level convergence toward high-probability behavioral channels and system-level context gravity from State, memory, history, and environment summaries. We introduce AutoPersonas, a multi-timescale life-environment engine for bounded persona-level recursive self-evolution. It separates environment-side Occurrences, accumulated Observations, and persona State. Its OSO loop admits divergent future-facing material while requiring evidence-governed absorption before State or reachability changes. A three-year compressed simulation exposed environment watermark shells, occurrence-hardening gaps, slow-change accumulation failures, recursive indecision, and weak relationship persistence. An eight-model 40-day stress test generated 1,600 events and found mean rolling 5-day action-category repetition of 95.2%-97.6%, with all models crossing 90% by day 11. Semantic re-keeping found 79.0%-88.0% macro-theme repetition across all direct-loop runs. In a same-runtime 40-day A/B, context-slice masking plus per-sample divergence targeting reduced macro-theme repetition from 61.8% to 36.3% and roughly doubled cumulative theme count. A juvenile-goblin fictional-world run reproduced the anti-fixation regime without hard real-world intrusions. These results support a bounded claim: separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption can reduce persona-environment self-locking while preserving identity continuity.

items.title: Researchers introduce a compete-then-collaborate framework where four AI teachers build a verifiable curriculum to improve a coding student beyond imitation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Compete Then Collaborate: Frontier AI Teachers Build a Verifiable Curriculum to Improve a Coding Student Beyond Imitation
items.summary: Researchers present a framework where four leading AI models—Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, and Gemini—are ranked by an execution-based judge and then collaborate to create a verifiable curriculum for training a coding student model, Qwen2.5-Coder. They find that while all teachers perform well on standard problems, harder tasks differentiate their abilities, but student improvement does not depend on teacher ranking. Imitation learning on verified solutions can degrade student performance, whereas reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves it significantly. The study highlights that AI teacher collaboration is more effective when focused on constructing a verifiable learning environment rather than pooling answers for imitation. The team also releases a reproducible on-premises pipeline for further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as teachers generating training data for smaller students. Prior multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods merge outputs without determining which frontier model teaches best, often relying on an LLM judge biased toward its own outputs. We introduce a compete-then-collaborate framework where four frontier AI teachers (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head by an execution-based judge (unit tests and stdin-stdout checks) with fairness controls, and then collaborate to build a verifiable curriculum for a student (Qwen2.5-Coder). We report three findings. (3) Using the same collaborative curriculum as a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment improves the student (from 5.9% to 8.8% peak on competition problems, a +49% relative gain), reversing SFT's direction. The value of AI-teacher collaboration lies not in pooling answers to imitate, but in jointly constructing a verifiable environment where the student learns by doing. We release a reproducible on-prem pipeline (NVIDIA GB10) with framework patches for running GRPO on a bleeding-edge stack.

items.originalTitle: MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters
items.summary: MentalHospital simulates the full psychiatric clinical workflow including interviewing, examination, diagnosis, and treatment planning, assessed through objective EHR comparisons and subjective clinical quality evaluations. The system incorporates MentalEval, five domain-specific evaluators trained with expert guidance to measure communication, professionalism, note quality, diagnostic rigor, and treatment appropriateness. Surveyed clinicians rated MentalHospital's clinical fidelity at 3.88 out of 5, and MentalEval showed strong alignment with expert judgments. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on isolated psychiatric tasks, including dialogue, diagnosis, and treatment planning, yet existing benchmarks rarely simulate complete psychiatric clinical encounters. Each encounter is assessed through a dual-track protocol that combines objective comparison against EHR-derived references with subjective assessment of clinical process quality. Survey responses from 22 clinicians support MentalHospital's clinical fidelity (3.88/5), while MentalEval achieves strong expert alignment with an average QWK of 0.944. Benchmarking shows that even the strongest LLM trails clinicians by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment as a key bottleneck.

items.title: Researchers distill an 8B reasoning model into a 0.6B on-device student for structured text enrichment, achieving faster processing and partial quality recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Different Teachers, Different Capabilities: Sub-1B On-Device Distillation for Structured Text Enrichment
items.summary:
Researchers distilled an 8-billion-parameter reasoning teacher model into a 0.6-billion-parameter student model for on-device structured text enrichment, mapping news articles to JSON objects with summaries and labels. The student runs significantly faster, processing articles in about 0.8 seconds compared to the teacher's 39 seconds, and recovers 58% of the quality gap in summaries, outperforming baseline methods like constrained decoding and few-shot prompting. The study included controls with a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline, evaluated by a blinded panel against full articles.

The results show that the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality, while the managed pipeline improves label diversity, and the non-reasoning teacher does not improve student performance beyond the untuned base. Some students trained on reasoning teachers fabricated content more often on short, thin-source articles, indicating a trade-off between writing quality and factual grounding. Because no single model excels in all aspects, the researchers propose a per-field routing map to optimize on-device text enrichment tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-volume structured extraction pays a large model's latency on every item, so distilling the task into a small on-device model is attractive: comparable output at a fraction of the time and cost. We measure what that distillation actually delivers, per sub-task. Each news article is mapped to one JSON object with a short summary and five categorical labels. We distill an 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B; QLoRA, three seeds), and add two teacher controls: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. A blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel scores every arm against the full article, alongside two non-distillation baselines, few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. The student runs at about 0.8 s per article against the teacher's 39 s, and recovers 58% of the base-to-teacher gap on summary quality, beating its primary baseline (constrained decoding) by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by a secondary +4.9. A same-size non-reasoning teacher trains a student no better than the untuned base, so the summary gain follows from the teacher's reasoning nature rather than its scale. Capabilities then split by teacher: the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality and the managed pipeline transfers label diversity, while a same-size instruction teacher's students stay more grounded on the 22 short, thin-source articles in the 93-item test set (74 versus 55 faithful), where the reasoning-lineage student fabricates. That grounding difference is a consistent ordering rather than a significant aggregate effect, and the subgroup is small, so we report it as a direction. Because no single engine wins every field, the deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment.

items.title: PolyUQuest launches verifiable, structure-aware web retrieval-augmented generation using heterogeneous graphs, improving accuracy and efficiency on Hong Kong Polytechnic University websites [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PolyUQuest: Verifiable Structure-Aware Web RAG over Heterogeneous Graphs
items.summary: PolyUQuest is a new retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that leverages a heterogeneous graph combining hyperlink topology, DOM hierarchy, and entity relations to preserve structural and semantic signals from web pages. It uses a two-tier router to select among three retrieval modes tailored to query needs, enabling verifiable answers with traceable sources. Evaluated on over 4,000 pages and tens of thousands of entities from Hong Kong Polytechnic University's official websites, PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in correctness, coverage, and faithfulness while reducing language model token usage per query. The system includes an interactive interface for inspecting answers and retrieval paths and is planned for deployment as a student-facing question-answering service at PolyU.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat web pages as flat text, losing the structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML. We present PolyUQuest, a verifiable, structure-aware web RAG framework built on a heterogeneous graph that unifies hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and entity-relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router dispatches each query to one of three retrieval modes matched to its structural need, including direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, and multi-hop entity reasoning. Every answer is fully verifiable, as each cited block carries its source page, heading path, and entity links so that users can trace any claim back to its structural evidence. We evaluate on the official websites of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), comprising 4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, and 37,680 relations, together with a multi-type evaluation benchmark. PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness, while consuming significantly fewer LLM tokens per query. The demonstration provides an interactive interface for inspecting cited answers, comparing retrieval traces across routing modes, and exploring evidence graph paths. PolyUQuest is being prepared for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU.

items.originalTitle: Understanding Axes of Difficulty For Long Context Tasks Via PredicateLongBench
items.summary: Researchers introduce PredicateLongBench, a benchmark designed to test large language models' long-context reasoning by identifying the longest contiguous subsequence of words satisfying specific predicates in long inputs. The benchmark includes synthetic and real-world data generation pipelines and explores various difficulty axes to assess multiple aspects of long-context understanding. Initial results show that leading models struggle as task difficulty increases, highlighting current limitations in long-context capabilities despite the tasks' conceptual simplicity and lack of reliance on model-generated content or judges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated rapidly improving long-context capabilities, prompting a wave of benchmarks designed to evaluate them. However, existing long-context evaluations - from Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) tests to more recent multi-hop reasoning and summarization tasks - predominantly measure average-case performance, and many are either saturated or lack robustness. Notably absent is a systematic way to probe how models perform as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along various axes. We address this gap by proposing PredicateLongBench, a benchmark that stress-tests long-context reasoning by asking models to identify the longest contiguous subsequence of words in a long input that satisfies given predicates/constraints (e.g., lexicographic ordering), drawn from a broader predicate class. The central innovation of our benchmark is the identification and systematic exploration of multiple different axes of difficulty which test multiple aspects of long context understanding. We provide two complementary generation pipelines - a fully synthetic setup using random word-like strings, and a real-world setup that samples words from natural documents while preserving their distributional properties. We find that frontier models struggle to perform well as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along our axes, demonstrating the utility of our benchmark in understanding the limitations of current long-context capabilities. Furthermore, the tasks in PredicateLongBench, though challenging, are conceptually simple and do not require LLM-based generations or judges.

items.originalTitle: Psychological Competence as a Missing Dimension in AI Evaluation
items.summary:
Current AI evaluation frameworks emphasize technical metrics like accuracy and robustness but often overlook the psychological impact of AI systems that interact directly with users through natural language. This paper introduces psychological competence as the ability of AI to appropriately support user cognition, emotional understanding, and behavior in context, highlighting factors such as tone, authority, and responsiveness.

The authors outline a conceptual framework for assessing psychological competence using scenario-based probes, structured human evaluations, and model-assisted methods. They argue that this dimension should be integrated into AI evaluation by developers, deployers, researchers, and regulators to better address the real-world effects of AI systems acting as advisors, coaches, tutors, or companions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current AI evaluation frameworks focus primarily on technical performance, including accuracy, robustness, reasoning ability, and policy compliance. These measures remain essential, but they are not sufficient for systems that interact directly with users through natural language. Human-facing AI systems are increasingly used as advisors, coaches, tutors, and companions. In these roles, their responses can shape how users reason, interpret emotions, form beliefs, calibrate trust, and make decisions. The relevant unit of evaluation is therefore not only the model, but the human-AI interaction. This paper introduces psychological competence as a missing dimension in AI evaluation. We define psychological competence as the capacity of a human-facing AI system to support user cognition, emotional interpretation, and behavioral decision-making in ways that are appropriate to the user, context, and purpose of the interaction. This includes interaction properties such as framing, tone, perceived authority, responsiveness, uncertainty handling, and conversational guidance. Existing evaluation approaches capture parts of this problem but rarely assess these psychological effects directly. Drawing on behavioral science and human-AI interaction research, we outline a conceptual framework for psychological competence and its core domains. Rather than proposing a specific benchmark, we define the construct, clarify its boundaries, and describe how it may be assessed through scenario-based probes, structured human evaluation, and model-assisted evaluation methods. We argue that psychological competence should become a core consideration for model providers, deploying organizations, researchers, and regulators concerned with the real-world effects of human-facing AI systems.

items.originalTitle: INTENT: An LSTM Framework for Vehicle Intention Prediction in Intersection Scenarios with Comprehensive Ablation Analysis
items.summary: The INTENT framework uses a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict vehicle intentions—going straight, turning left, or turning right—at intersections two seconds before the event occurs. This approach aims to improve autonomous vehicle safety and agility by enabling better interpretation of driver intentions in complex scenarios such as intersections, roundabouts, and emergency stops. The model was extensively tested with ablation studies on the InD dataset, achieving 99.71% accuracy. Vehicle intention prediction is critical for timely evasive actions and can also enhance trajectory prediction by conditioning on predicted intentions.

items.originalTitle: Blind-Spots-Bench: Evaluating Blind Spots in Multimodal Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed Blind-Spots-Bench, a new benchmark designed to reveal persistent blind spots in modern multimodal AI models by testing them on tasks that are simple for humans but challenging for AI. The benchmark includes 235 samples derived from student questions, annotated with structured reference solutions, and covers language, vision-language, and image-generation models. An automated grading pipeline was created to evaluate both open-weight and closed-source models, revealing that closed-source frontier models outperform open-weight ones by about 10% despite similar performance on existing benchmarks. The analysis also found no single model excels across all task types, highlighting ongoing challenges and the benchmark's value as a diagnostic tool for identifying specific AI weaknesses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern AI models achieve strong performance on many established benchmarks, yet they still fail on tasks that humans find almost trivial, such as manipulating a string or drawing a dog with five legs. These examples suggest that existing benchmarks may under-measure persistent blind spots in current systems. We introduce $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$, a benchmark designed to expose such blind spots through tasks that appear simple for humans but remain challenging for modern AI. We collect raw questions from students in an AI course, clean and annotate them with structured reference solutions, and propose a task taxonomy tailored to the resulting dataset of 235 samples. We further develop an automated grading pipeline to evaluate a wide range of models, including open-weight and closed-source language, vision-language, and image-generation models. Our analysis on $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ reveals that closed-source frontier models can substantially outperform open-weight models with even $\approx10\%$ gap, even when they attain comparable performance on existing benchmarks. A more fine-grained analysis shows that no single model dominates across all task types, and that some tasks remain challenging for all evaluated models. These results highlight the value of $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ as a diagnostic stress test for identifying concrete weaknesses in current modern models.

items.title: Researchers introduce MobiDiff, a discrete diffusion framework for generating synthetic human mobility data with semantic multi-channel modeling, showing improved speed and fidelity over prior methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MobiDiff: Semantic-Aware Multi-Channel Discrete Diffusion for Human Mobility Data Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MobiDiff, an end-to-end discrete diffusion model that generates synthetic human mobility data by directly denoising multi-channel semantic skeletons representing spatial, activity, and temporal information. This approach avoids complex interpolation and latent trace construction used in previous diffusion-based methods, enabling efficient and interpretable modeling of discrete semantic events in mobility data.

MobiDiff was evaluated on large-scale datasets from Atlanta, Boston, and Seattle, demonstrating competitive preservation of trajectory lengths and temporal intervals while being 5.3 times faster on average than the state-of-the-art GeoGen method during inference. The results suggest that discrete diffusion offers a promising framework for privacy-preserving and efficient synthetic mobility data generation useful for transportation optimization and urban planning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human mobility data are essential for transportation optimization, urban planning, and resource allocation, yet real-world mobility data are costly to collect and difficult to share due to privacy concerns. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown promise in synthesizing realistic mobility patterns, but they typically rely on continuous or latent spatio-temporal traces, limiting their ability to natively model discrete semantic events with explicit region, activity, time, and interval structures. To address this issue, we introduce MobiDiff, an end-to-end discrete diffusion framework that efficiently generates mobility data by directly denoising multi-channel semantic skeletons, avoiding the costly interpolation, latent trace construction, and coarse-to-fine realization pipelines widely used in existing diffusion-based methods. Specifically, MobiDiff decomposes each human check-in event into spatial, activity, and temporal channels, and employs structured event-, group-, and channel-level masking to jointly capture trajectory-level mobility patterns and within-event dependencies. We evaluate generation fidelity, privacy-preserving, and efficiency on three large-scale real-world datasets from Atlanta, Boston, and Seattle. Results show that MobiDiff effectively preserves trajectory length and temporal interval distributions while remaining competitive across broader mobility statistics; it is also much faster than state-of-the-art methods, e.g., 5.3$\times$ faster than GeoGen on average during inference. These findings suggest that discrete diffusion offers an interpretable and efficient framework for synthetic mobility data generation.

items.title: FedOPAL introduces one-shot federated learning with analytic visual prompt tuning to improve feature alignment and reduce server-side costs in edge intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FedOPAL: One-Shot Federated Learning via Analytic Visual Prompt Tuning
items.summary:
FedOPAL is a new federated learning framework designed to address communication bandwidth bottlenecks and computational costs in edge intelligence. It uses visual prompts as feature rectifiers to correct heterogeneous data distributions, enabling efficient gradient-free aggregation with least-squares closed-form solutions while maintaining accuracy comparable to iterative methods.

The framework overcomes limitations of existing analytical federated learning approaches that assume static features, which fail under non-independent and identically distributed data. Experimental results demonstrate that FedOPAL significantly outperforms original analytical methods on multiple benchmarks and eliminates server-side training costs, offering a scalable solution for collaborative learning with large models on edge devices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the widespread deployment of basic models in edge intelligence, communication bandwidth has become a core bottleneck restricting the scalability of federated learning. Although one-shot federated learning alleviates this problem by minimizing communication rounds, existing iterative fine-tuning or knowledge distillation methods still face challenges such as high server-side computational costs and hyperparameter sensitivity. Analytical federated learning achieves efficient gradientfree aggregation using least-squares closed-form solutions, but in environments with non-independent and identically distributed data, its static feature assumptions fail, leading to feature manifold misalignment and severely impairing model performance. To address this contradiction, this paper proposes the FedOPAL framework. This framework adapts the visual prompts as feature rectifiers, actively correcting the feature distribution of heterogeneous data to a linearly separable space by applying local proximal constraints, thereby satisfying the theoretical assumptions of analytical federated learning. Experimental results show that FedOPAL not only significantly outperforms the original analytical methods on several benchmarks, but also achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art iterative methods while maintaining zero server-side training costs, providing a new engineering paradigm for efficient collaboration of large models on the edge.

items.title: Researchers identify knowledge-circuit misalignment as cause of generalization failures in fine-tuned large language models, proposing self-patching to improve reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Mechanistically Understanding Why Memorized Knowledge Fails to Generalize in Large Language Model Finetuning
items.summary: Researchers studied why large language models (LLMs) quickly memorize new facts during fine-tuning but fail to apply them in downstream reasoning tasks, defining this as the Knowing--Using Gap. They introduced self-patching, a technique that locates internal activations where relocating representations improves generalization failures, supporting a hypothesis that memorized knowledge is not routed to computation-effective layers. Their heuristic strategy recovers 58–75% of potential improvement in generalization, with experiments confirming robustness across domains.

They introduced self-patching, a technique that locates internal activations where relocating representations improves generalization failures, supporting a hypothesis that memorized knowledge is not routed to computation-effective layers. Their heuristic strategy recovers 58–75% of potential improvement in generalization, with experiments confirming robustness across domains.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs to inject new knowledge faces a critical challenge: LLMs can quickly memorize new facts, yet fail to use them for downstream reasoning tasks. We formalize this failure as the \textit{\textbf{Knowing--Using Gap}}, characterized by an accuracy gap and a temporal lag between memorization and generalization. To understand this phenomenon, we fine-tune LLMs with unseen knowledge and monitor the spatial permeation dynamics of the knowledge internally using a novel intervention technique called self-patching. Self-patching identifies activation locations where relocating representations substantially improves failed generalization cases. These results are consistent with a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis: memorized representations can exist internally but may not be routed to computation-effective layers. To demonstrate the practicality of this diagnostic finding, we design a simple heuristic strategy which recovers 58--75\% of the oracle headroom in generalization failure. Experiments are done cross-domain for the robustness of this finding.

items.originalTitle: Game Theory Driven Multi-Agent Framework Mitigates Language Model Hallucination
items.summary: Researchers introduce G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework combining Bayesian and game theory principles to improve reasoning in lightweight language models used in scientific domains. By synthesizing a large specialized dataset and enforcing domain constraints, their 7-billion-parameter model OmniChem matches GPT-4o mini performance on chemistry benchmarks while reducing hallucinations by 79%. The model also demonstrates advanced capabilities in molecular design and synthesis planning. This approach offers a scalable method to enhance reasoning and accelerate knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The application of lightweight Large Language Models in rule-based scientific domains remains severely limited by their tendency to mimic linguistic patterns rather than reproduce axiomatic reasoning, causing frequent hallucinations. Here, we show that G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework integrating Bayesian and team game principles, establishes an automated closed-loop for high-quality data synthesis and model training. By forcing the internalization of domain constraints through structured reasoning, we synthesized a specialized corpus of 363,045 chains-of-thought and 199,589 question-answer pairs. The resulting 7B model OmniChem achieves performance parity with GPT 4o mini on custom benchmarks and ChemBench while exhibiting a 79.46% reduction in hallucinations relative to its base architecture. We further demonstrate the advanced capabilities of OmniChem in molecular design and synthesis planning. This work establishes a scalable paradigm utilizing adaptive multi-agents to overcome inherent reasoning deficiencies, offering a feasible pathway for accelerating knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

items.title: OmniFood-Bench evaluates vision-language models on nutrient reasoning and personalized health advice using MM-Food-100K dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OmniFood-Bench: Evaluating VLMs for Nutrient Reasoning and Personalized Health Advice
items.summary: Researchers introduce OmniFood-Bench, a benchmark designed to assess vision-language models (VLMs) on their ability to perform nutrient reasoning and provide personalized dietary advice. The benchmark tests models across three levels: basic perception of ingredients and cooking methods, quantitative reasoning for portion size and nutritional profiling, and safety-critical recommendations for disease-specific diets. Six state-of-the-art VLMs, including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B, were evaluated, revealing that while models can accurately identify dishes, they struggle with estimating mass and often generate incorrect advice for high-risk diabetic patients. This work highlights challenges in deploying autonomous agents for public health and sets a standard for evaluating their trustworthiness.
items.description: Researchers introduce OmniFood-Bench, a benchmark designed to assess vision-language models (VLMs) on their ability to perform nutrient reasoning and provide personalized dietary advice. The benchmark tests models across three levels: basic perception of ingredients and cooking methods, quantitative reasoning for portion size and nutritional profiling, and safety-critical recommendations for disease-specific diets. Six state-of-the-art VLMs, including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B, were evaluated, revealing that while models can accurately identify dishes, they struggle with estimating mass and often generate incorrect advice for high-risk diabetic patients. This work highlights challenges in deploying autonomous agents for public health and sets a standard for evaluating their trustworthiness.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid integration of Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into critical infrastructure promises to revolutionize personalized healthcare and dietary management. However, in the domain of food systems, autonomous agents face a unique and persistent challenge: the "Systemic Information Asymmetry" between visual appearance and intrinsic nutritional composition. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on coarse-grained classification tasks, such as food category recognition, which fail to evaluate the intricate reasoning chain required for real-world dietary management -- specifically, the ability to traverse from identifying hidden ingredients to estimating physical mass, and finally synthesizing safety-critical medical advice. In this paper, we introduce OmniFood-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from the MM-Food-100K dataset. Unlike previous works, OmniFood-Bench evaluates VLMs across three progressive capabilities: Basic Perception (Ingredients & Cooking Methods), Quantitative Reasoning (Portion Size & Nutritional Profiling), and Safety-Critical Advisory (Disease-Specific Recommendations). We evaluate six state-of-the-art VLMs, including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B. Our extensive experiments reveal a startling "Semantic-Physical Gap": while models achieve near-human accuracy in naming dishes, they exhibit catastrophic failure in mass estimation and frequently hallucinate benign advice for high-risk diabetic profiles. This work establishes a rigorous standard for trustworthiness in autonomous agents deployed for public health. The code and datasets are available in: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniFood-Bench-7D0B

items.title: Researchers apply JEPA-style predictive learning to JA4-derived network fingerprints using a Transformer model trained on 397K samples from JA4DB and CIC-IDS-2017 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Applying JEPA-Style Predictive Learning to JA4-Derived Network Fingerprints
items.summary:
Researchers developed JA4-JEPA, a Transformer-based model trained on JA4, JA4H, JA4S, and JA4X subfields from JA4DB and CIC-IDS-2017 datasets, totaling approximately 397,000 samples. The model uses JEPA-style predictive learning, which matches latent predictions to target encoder outputs instead of regenerating inputs, a method previously successful in images and video.

The learned representations were evaluated with a frozen k-nearest neighbors probe on protocol-family classification tasks across TLS, DNS, and SSH protocols. On 39,416 heldout samples, the model achieved a cosine similarity of 0.9899 and a kNN accuracy of 0.9220, indicating that JEPA-style learning can produce effective embeddings from JA4-derived network fingerprints even when view overlap across sources is incomplete.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.08465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I-JEPA and V-JEPA learn by matching latent predictions to target encoder outputs rather than regenerating the original input, and this has worked well for images and video. We explore whether the same objective works for compact network fingerprints. We built JA4-JEPA, a Transformer-based model trained on JA4, JA4H, JA4S, and JA4X subfields drawn from JA4DB and CIC-IDS- 2017. The training data combines roughly 397K samples from both sources, though no single sample contains all four view families. We evaluated the learned representations with a frozen kNN probe on protocol-family classification across TLS, DNS, and SSH. On 39,416 heldout samples the model achieved a cosine similarity of 0.9899 and a kNN accuracy of 0.9220. These results indicate that JEPA-style predictive learning can produce useful embeddings from JA4-derived fingerprints, even with incomplete view overlap across sources. Keywords: JA4, network fingerprinting, JEPA, predictive representation learning, self-supervised learning
